title: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
summary: A game creates and destroys objects constantly: bullets, particles, enemies, pickups. This lesson puts the chapter together into the structures engines use for them: dense arrays with swap-and-pop, **object pools** with free lists, and **generational handles** that let code refer to an object safely even after it has been destroyed and its slot reused.
markdown:
## What games need A shooter might fire 50 bullets a second, each living for a second or two. A particle effect might spawn thousands of sparks. The container holding them must: 1. **Loop fast**, every frame, over everything alive. 2. **Add and remove cheaply**, many times per frame. 3. **Let other code refer to an object** (the missile's target, the player's selected unit) without that reference turning into a dangling pointer when the object dies. No single standard container does all three. These are the patterns engines combine. ## Pattern 1: a dense vector with swap-and-pop Keep live objects side by side in a `std::vector`, and remove with swap-and-pop (lesson 3.07): ```cpp #include #include struct Bullet { float x; float speed; float life; }; void update(std::vector& bullets, float dt) { for (std::size_t i{ 0 }; i < bullets.size(); ) { Bullet& b{ bullets[i] }; b.x += b.speed * dt; b.life -= dt; if (b.life <= 0) { bullets[i] = bullets.back(); // swap-and-pop: the last bullet takes this slot bullets.pop_back(); // don't advance i: the moved bullet needs updating too } else ++i; } } int main() { std::vector bullets{ { 0, 10, 0.05f }, { 0, 20, 1 }, { 0, 30, 0.05f }, { 0, 40, 1 } }; update(bullets, 0.1f); for (const Bullet& b : bullets) std::cout << b.speed << ' '; std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` 40 20 ``` Fast to loop over, cheap to remove from. But it fails requirement 3: an object's position in the vector changes whenever another object is removed, so neither a pointer nor an index to it stays valid. ## Pattern 2: a pool with a free list A **pool** allocates a fixed array of slots once and never moves them. Each slot is either in use or free. The free slots form a linked list threaded through the slots themselves (an intrusive list, lesson 3.06), so finding a free slot is "take the head of the free list" and freeing one is "push it back on". ``` slots: [0: bullet] [1: free → 3] [2: bullet] [3: free → 4] [4: free → end] freeHead = 1 ``` No heap allocations after start-up, objects never move, so a slot index stays valid while its object lives. Looping over the live objects means skipping free slots, which is slower than a dense vector when the pool is mostly empty. ## The remaining problem: stale references Suppose a missile stores "my target is slot 7". The target dies and slot 7 is freed. A moment later a new enemy is spawned into slot 7. The missile now chases the wrong enemy, and nothing tells it so. Index 7 is a dangling reference, just as a pointer would have been. ## Pattern 3: generational handles The fix is to give every slot a **generation** counter, incremented each time the slot is freed. A **handle** to an object is the pair (slot index, generation at the time). To use a handle, check that the slot's current generation still matches: ```mermaid flowchart LR H1["missile's handle
slot 7, gen 3"] --> S7["slot 7
gen 3: goblin"] S7 -->|"goblin dies: gen becomes 4"| S7b["slot 7
gen 4: free"] S7b -->|"bat spawned into slot 7"| S7c["slot 7
gen 4: bat"] H1 -.->|"lookup: 3 ≠ 4, so the goblin is gone"| X["nullptr"] ``` The missile's handle says generation 3, the slot now says 4, so the lookup returns null: "your target no longer exists". The new bat in slot 7 gets handles with generation 4, which work normally. ```cpp struct Handle { std::uint32_t index; std::uint32_t generation; }; ``` Eight bytes, trivially copyable, safe to store anywhere, safe to save to a file, and impossible to dangle. This is the approach used by most modern engines for entities, resources and anything else whose lifetime other systems cannot predict. The practice task is to build one. ## Choosing | Need | Use | |---|---| | Many short-lived objects nobody else refers to (particles, bullets) | Dense `std::vector` with swap-and-pop | | Objects referred to from elsewhere (enemies, units, items in the world) | A pool with generational handles | | Both fast loops and stable handles | A pool for identity plus a dense array of the data, with an index map between them (a "slot map" or "sparse set": the same idea, one step further) | | Few objects, created rarely | Whatever is simplest: `std::vector>` is fine | Chapter 10 uses these in its entity-component system. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Advancing the index after swap-and-pop > The element moved into slot `i` has not been processed yet. Only advance when nothing was removed. > [!warning] Storing raw pointers to pooled objects for later > They stay valid in memory, but may point at a different object after reuse. Store handles. > [!warning] Letting the generation counter wrap round quickly > With a 32-bit counter it would take billions of reuses of one slot, which is fine. An 8-bit counter wraps after 256 and can, rarely, let a stale handle match again. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What three things does a container of game objects usually need to do well? - Sort the objects, save them to disk and print them - Keep objects in creation order, never move them, and free them automatically + Loop quickly over live objects, add and remove them cheaply, and let other code refer to an object safely > The patterns in the lesson each trade these three off differently. ? How does a generational handle detect that its object is gone? - It holds a pointer and checks whether it is null + The slot's generation changes on free, so the handle's no longer matches - The pool keeps a list of every handle ever made and deletes them - It asks the operating system whether the memory is still allocated > The handle remembers the generation from when it was made, so a reused slot is recognised as a different object. ? Why are handles safer to store than pointers? - Handles are smaller than pointers - Handles keep the object alive - Handles cannot be copied + A stale handle is caught on lookup; a stale pointer is not > The lookup turns a silent memory bug into a clear "the object is gone" result. ? Why does a dense vector with swap-and-pop not give objects stable references? - Vectors cannot be indexed + Removing one moves another into its slot - Swap-and-pop allocates memory > The last element is moved to fill the gap, so its index changes. ? What does a pool's free list link together? - The live objects, in creation order - Every slot, used or not + The unused slots, through an index stored in each > Allocating takes the head of the free list; freeing pushes the slot back on. ? A handle says (slot 12, generation 5). The pool's slot 12 has generation 6. What does a lookup return? - The object in slot 12 + Nothing: the object the handle referred to has been destroyed - The object, after updating the handle > A different generation means the slot has been freed since the handle was made. ```
ideas:
- Change the bullet example's `update` to advance `i` every time and find which bullet is skipped.
- On paper, run this sequence on a pool of 4 slots and write down the free list and generations after each step: create A, create B, destroy A, create C, destroy B.
- Think about how you would loop over only the live objects in a pool quickly when it is nearly empty.
